newsitem.title: GERMANY: German miners protest, then retreat awaiting talks.
newsitem.headline: German miners protest, then retreat awaiting talks.

text.p: Thousands of angry German miners paralysed Bonn for the third day running on Wednesday but most looked ready to retreat to let their union leader try again to negotiate planned subsidy cuts with Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

About 6,500 pit workers from the Saar state on the French border held a raucous rally in Bonn but most said they would reluctantly heed union leader Hans Berger's appeal to wait in neighbouring Cologne until the talks started on Thursday.
"If we all stay here, we won't get our negotiations tomorrow either," Berger beseeched his members hoarsely.
The men shouted back defiant choruses of "We're staying here!" and taunted Berger with calls of "Judas, Judas!". But the crowd later calmed down and began to disperse.

Kohl, who put off meeting Berger on Tuesday because of the unruly protests, promised to meet him on Thursday but insisted that his proposed cuts in subsidy from nine billion marks ($5.3 billion) to 3.8 billion marks by 2005 were fair.
"I want the coal industry to survive and experts say that's possible at a lower level (than today)," he said. "But we have to go step-by-step (with the cuts) between now and 2005."

In an unrelated protest, 5,000 construction workers marched in Berlin to protest against job losses in their stricken sector. A group smashed cabbage heads to highlight their opposition to Kohl, whose name means cabbage in German.
Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) chairman Oskar Lafontaine, premier of the coal-producing Saar state, gave a firebreathing speech against Kohl's coal policy at the rally.
"The Saar state and the whole country stands behind you," he shouted to the cheering miners. "We need to show Kohl and his whole crew what losing their jobs feels like. "

Bracing for another day of hordes of burly miners roaring in on motorcycles and buses, Bonn beefed up security measures on Wednesday, ordering in federal border guards to replace the city police officers who had been monitoring the crowd.

On Tuesday, a Bonn demonstration by miners from Germany's Ruhr valley coal-and-steel heartland spilled over briefly into violence, prompting Kohl to push back the planned negotiations with the union at short notice.
Those miners obeyed Berger's call that they leave Bonn, but no sooner had they gone than another 3,000 or so Saar miners arrived to keep up a night-time vigil.

"I think we should stick it out until tomorrow but if the union says it would be better for the talks if we left, then I'll go out to Cologne," said Richard Rohman, who arrived in Bonn on Tuesday evening from Saar.

"We don't want to fight with the government. We're peaceful citizens," said Bernhardt Meiser, a veteran of 25 years in the pits. "Since we're here, I don't really want to leave but I will if that's what the union says we should do."
Yet a handful of pit workers said they would stay no matter what the call from the union. "If we leave, I know we'll get a lousy deal," said Michael Zick. "This is my last chance."

The free-market Free Democrats (FDP), Kohl's junior coalition partners, said they were prepared to hold their ground against the massive protests but hinted they could be more flexible on the timetable for phasing out the subsidies.

Miners in Germany's 18 pits walked out on Friday after Bonn announced its proposals for subsidy cuts. The government argues it can no longer afford to pay over nine billion marks a year to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is over three times the world market price.
But mining union IG Bergbau says the plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
Kohl's Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told ZDF television late on Tuesday that the government was standing by its plan, but he added that he saw the potential for an agreement with the union.
The Social Democrats, who rule the two main coal mining states, have strongly backed the miners.

But they said for the first time on Wednesday they would not maintain a boycott of talks with the government on tax reform, even if Kohl failed to make a satisfactory offer to the pit workers. ($ = 1.708 German Marks)
